items.ownerBrief: One product call now queued at /create-prd (Owner: User) from 14.01 CX-01 #5: when a buyer edits their rig after committing but before the first byte, the live verdict can flip while the verdict recorded against their order cannot. Nothing breaks — delivery does not gate on compatibility and a false badge refunds unconditionally — so the only question is whether the withdrawal-waiver screen should carry a compatibility warning when the verdict has moved since purchase. Surfacing it interrupts the one screen the buyer is legally required to read, on a right they are about to waive, and will cost some completions; staying silent means the store knew and said nothing on the last screen before the money became final.

items.ownerBrief:
Two product calls now queued at /create-prd (Owner: User), neither answerable without you.

1. 14.02.03 Q-04 — may a bridged licence (iLok/PACE) be deposited into a third-party account that is not the buyer's? Permitted, blocked at checkout, or treated as a transfer under 14.06.01's vendor policy registry. The record already expresses purchaser ≠ holder (14.02.01 D-05), and at launch checkout sets holder = purchaser with no gift path offered — but a bridged deposit is the one path that can hand a licence to someone else without WeJammin recording the divergence, and it is irreversible in a system we do not control. Blocking means policing an account identity we cannot verify. Permitting creates an untracked gift/transfer that bypasses 14.06 and the vendor's own transfer policy. Treating it as a transfer imports escrow machinery (14.06.02) onto a licence we cannot enforce. This rides with 14.02.01 Q-01 (does a gift flow ship at all).

2. 14.02.04 Q-04 — when a chargeback was card fraud against the buyer, what restores the entitlement the reversal revoked, and on whose evidence? The routing is already settled (a chargeback is a revocation, never a blacklist; every action carries reason, notice and an appeal into domain 24), so what is missing is the standard the appeal applies. The issuer's own fraud finding is the natural proof but arrives on the network's schedule, not the buyer's; a police report is a heavy ask for a £79 plugin; letting the buyer simply re-pay restores access fastest but reads as being charged twice for one theft. Distinct from who eats the loss, which is 14.02.01 Q-03.
